title: Dye-based fluorescent organic nanoparticles: from chemistry to biology
content: Luminescent nanoparticles are readily becoming indispensable tools for bioimaging. Among the many luminescent nanoparticle variants available to date, dye-based fluorescent organic nanoparticles known as dFONs appear to be less known to the biological community than others. Yet, these single component objects, prepared by nano-aggregation of molecular dyes in water, offer several much sought-after properties. These include spontaneous water compatibility and high brightness, both necessary for state-of-the-art bioimaging. dFONs also display specificities such as extreme tunability, unique vectorisation capabilities and many other advantages to be discussed here. Since the last review of the dFONs litterature, dating back over a decade, significant advances have been made towards (i) tuning dFONs absorption and emission to the biological optical window, (ii) demanding bioimaging modalities such as single particle tracking and sensing and (iii) elegantly designed drug-delivery systems. Thanks to these recent developments, dFONs research should be blooming. Yet, it appears to be stuck at a proof-of-concept stage. We will discuss why this may be and propose avenues for taking up this exciting field's challenges. In doing so, we strive to help with dFONs dissemination to communities of both chemists interested in their design and biologists interested in their use.
